items.stem: The internal value of money refers to
options: the quantity of money in circulation
its purchasing power over domestic goods and services
its exchange rate against other currencies
items.answer: its purchasing power over domestic goods and services
items.markingKey: Falls when the domestic price level rises.

items.stem: Explain how a fall in the internal value of money can lead to a fall in its external value.
items.answer: Domestic inflation makes exports dearer and imports relatively cheaper, so demand for the currency falls and supply rises; under a floating rate it depreciates.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: inflation reduces competitiveness; 1 mark: demand/supply of currency; 1 mark: depreciation [3]

items.stem: Explain how a depreciation can reduce the internal value of money.
items.answer: Imported goods and raw materials become more expensive, raising costs and consumer prices (imported inflation), and higher demand for exports adds demand-pull pressure.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: dearer imports/costs; 1 mark: higher price level [2]

items.stem: The price level in Ostrelia rises by 25%. Calculate the percentage fall in the internal value (purchasing power) of money.
items.markingKey: Purchasing power = 100/1.25 = 80; fall = 20%.

items.stem: Over a year, prices rise by 50% in Umbria Nova and by 3% in its trading partners. At the start of the year, $1 (partner currency) = 10 units of Umbria Nova’s currency. (a) Calculate the fall in the internal value of Umbria Nova’s money. (b) Using relative purchasing power parity, calculate the exchange rate needed to keep Umbria Nova’s exports equally competitive. (c) Explain what happens to competitiveness if the exchange rate does not change.
items.answer: (a) 33.33% (b) about 14.56 units per $1 (a depreciation of 45.6%) (c) Umbria Nova’s real exchange rate appreciates: exports become dearer abroad and imports cheaper, worsening the current account.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 − 1/1.5 [1]; (b) 10 × 1.5/1.03 [2]; (c) real appreciation, loss of competitiveness [2].

items.stem: Extract: Rovania’s currency depreciated by 15% last year. Inflation rose from 2% to 5%, partly because 40% of consumer goods are imported. The current account deficit narrowed and export firms expanded output. (a) Explain the link between the depreciation and the rise in inflation. (b) Explain one conflict between macroeconomic objectives shown in the extract.
items.answer: (a) Imported goods and inputs dearer (cost-push); higher export demand (demand-pull). (b) External balance improving vs inflation rising.

items.stem: The external value of money is measured by
items.answer: the exchange rate
items.markingKey: Value of the currency in terms of other currencies.

items.stem: Prices in Istrana rose by 15% last year while its exchange rate was fixed. Explain what happened to the internal and external value of its currency and to its competitiveness.
items.answer: Internal value (purchasing power) fell by about 13%; the nominal external value was unchanged, so the real exchange rate appreciated and exports became less competitive.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: internal value fall; 1 mark: real appreciation/competitiveness [2]

items.stem: Prices in Jovania rose by 15% last year while its exchange rate was fixed. Explain what happened to the internal and external value of its currency and to its competitiveness.

items.markingKey: 1 mark: internal value fall; 1 mark: real appreciation/competitiveness [2]

items.stem: The price level in Valdoria rises by 50%. Calculate the percentage fall in the internal value (purchasing power) of money.
items.markingKey: Purchasing power = 100/1.5 = 66.67; fall = 33.33%.

items.stem: Over a year, prices rise by 20% in Rovania and by 2% in its trading partners. At the start of the year, $1 (partner currency) = 4 units of Rovania’s currency. (a) Calculate the fall in the internal value of Rovania’s money. (b) Using relative purchasing power parity, calculate the exchange rate needed to keep Rovania’s exports equally competitive. (c) Explain what happens to competitiveness if the exchange rate does not change.
items.answer: (a) 16.67% (b) about 4.71 units per $1 (a depreciation of 17.6%) (c) Rovania’s real exchange rate appreciates: exports become dearer abroad and imports cheaper, worsening the current account.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 − 1/1.2 [1]; (b) 4 × 1.2/1.02 [2]; (c) real appreciation, loss of competitiveness [2].

items.stem: Ostrelia’s currency has lost a quarter of its value against the US dollar in a year. Evaluate the view that a fall in the external value of a currency will always cause inflation.
items.answer: Arguments for: Depreciation raises import prices and export demand. Arguments against / evaluation: Depends on import share, pass-through, spare capacity, inflation expectations and firms absorbing costs. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: Rapid economic growth driven by consumer spending is likely to
options: worsen the current account as imports rise
items.answer: worsen the current account as imports rise
items.markingKey: Higher incomes raise imports (income elasticity of demand for imports).

items.stem: Explain how a current account deficit can slow economic growth.
items.answer: Net imports are a withdrawal from the circular flow, reducing AD; financing may require higher interest rates; loss of domestic industry.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: withdrawal/lower AD; 1 mark: financing/higher interest rates [2]

items.stem: Explain how economic growth could improve the current account.
items.answer: If growth is supply-side or export-led, productivity rises, lowering costs and improving competitiveness, so exports grow faster than imports.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: productivity/competitiveness; 1 mark: exports rise [2]

items.answer: −$220 billion

Calculate the balance on trade in goods and services and the current account balance.
items.answer: Goods and services balance = −$70 billion; current account = −$95 billion.

items.stem: Extract: Fendaria’s currency depreciated by 20% last year. Inflation rose from 3% to 7%, partly because 40% of consumer goods are imported. items.answer: (a) Imported goods and inputs dearer (cost-push); higher export demand (demand-pull). (b) Exports cheaper abroad, imports dearer; Marshall–Lerner condition met after the J-curve period.

items.answer: Rising incomes increase spending on imports (income elasticity of demand for imports is often above 1) faster than exports grow.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: income-related imports; 1 mark: exports grow more slowly [2]

items.stem: Balance of payments data for Merania ($ billion): exports of goods 400; imports of goods 320; exports of services 120; imports of services 90; primary income credits 30; primary income debits 40; net secondary income -10. Calculate the balance on trade in goods and services and the current account balance. Real GDP then grows by 3% and the income elasticity of demand for imports of goods is 2.5. With other items unchanged, calculate the new goods imports and current account balance.
items.answer: Goods and services balance = $110 billion; current account = $90 billion. Imports rise by 7.5% to 344; current account becomes $66 billion.

items.stem: Selmaria has run a current account deficit of about 4% of GDP for ten years. (a) Explain the links between the balance of payments and economic growth. (b) Discuss whether a current account deficit is always harmful to an economy.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Deficits reduce AD, require financing, risk crises. (b) Case for the view: Deficits reduce AD, require financing, risk crises. Case against / evaluation: Deficits financed by FDI for investment can raise growth; temporary deficits in booms; surplus countries may have weak demand. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: Explain why there may be a conflict between economic growth and a stable current account.
items.answer: Faster growth raises incomes and imports (high YED for imports), and may raise inflation, reducing competitiveness, so the current account deteriorates.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: imports rise; 1 mark: inflation/competitiveness [2]

items.stem: Explain why a policy to reduce income inequality might conflict with economic growth.
items.answer: Higher progressive taxes and benefits may reduce incentives to work, save and invest, and raise the cost of government, slowing growth (though better education can help growth).
